extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate English readers; readers of The Spectator interested in manners, morals, and literary taste
extracted.subtask_description: Short, didactic-satirical periodical essays offering commentary on manners, literature, religion, and social rank; mixes moral instruction, literary criticism, and comic sketches. Useful as guidance for composing or interpreting genteel eighteenth-century satire and essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication precedence (pamphleteers/octavos/folio)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have had so strict a regard to the Ceremonial which prevails in the Learned World, that I never presumed to take place of a Pamphleteer till my daily Papers were gathered into those two first Volumes... six Octavo's have at all times been look'd upon as an Equivalent to a Folio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts a customary rule of literary precedence: periodical papers should not claim the status of full authorship until collected in volumes; printers and booksellers arrange social/physical precedence (who 'takes the Wall') according to the perceived merits/format (octavo vs folio). This is presented as an established ceremonial convention to be observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social rank among learned professions and lay orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Precedency is settled among the three Learned Professions... every Doctor in each of these Professions... though not so high as Knights, yet a Degree above Squires; this last Order of Men being the illiterate Body of the Nation, are consequently thrown together into a Class below the three Learned Professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normative ordering of social ranks is given: learned professions outrank squires; writers should recognize and observe these conventional distinctions. The text also counsels leniency toward ignorant squires ('Their Want of Learning...may in some measure extenuate their Misdemeanour').

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage and genre precedence (tragedy over comedy; tragi-comedy between)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among [actors] it is a standing and uncontroverted Principle, that a Tragedian always takes place of a Comedian... 'Once a King, and always a King'. By a Parity of Reason, all Writers of Tragedy look upon it as their due to be seated, served, or saluted before Comick Writers: Those who deal in Tragi-Comedy usually taking their Seats between the Authors of either Side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes a hierarchical etiquette for theatrical persons and dramatic writers: tragic actors and tragic/heroic poets claim precedence over comic and burlesque writers. The passage records this as a recognized 'maxim' and notes historical disputes (Aristotle vs Dryden) as background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive guideline for small/diminutive epithets in poetry (Adrian's lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The diminutive Epithets of 'Vagula, Blandula'...appear not to me as Expressions of Levity, but rather of Endearment and Concern; such as we find in Catullus... where they are used to express the utmost Love and Tenderness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting classical/dying utterances, consider cultural usage: diminutives may signal tenderness and seriousness rather than levity. Read context (author's situation, beliefs) before labeling lines as 'gay' or frivolous. The passage uses Adrian's 'Animula vagula' to argue for a sober, affectionate reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote other men's merit (cultivate and publish excellence)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a very honest Action to be studious to produce other Men's Merit... I claim to my self the Merit of having extorted excellent Productions from a Person of the greatest Abilities... animated a few young Gentlemen into worthy Pursuits... undermined the Interests of Ignorance, Vice, and Folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prescriptive ethic for literary/cultural actors: turn personal ambition toward promoting worthy work, encourage talented peers and youth, and use one's influence to advance learning and virtue. The author treats this as a laudable aim and a standard of responsible criticism/editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual veneration of the Divine (religious decorum as moral practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: We should often refresh our Minds with the Thought of him, and annihilate our selves before him... such a constant and uninterrupted Awe and Veneration... which is in reality a kind of incessant Prayer, and reasonable Humiliation of the Soul before him who made it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends regular contemplative practice as an ethical/psychological means to curb pride and stimulate religious virtue; frames habitual worship as both reverence and moral discipline with social and personal benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using God's name in trivial speech or works of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: That prevailing Impiety of using his Name on the most trivial Occasions... those who admit it into the most familiar Questions and Assertions, ludicrous Phrases and Works of Humour... The very mention of it exposes it sufficiently to those in whom the Light of Nature, not to say Religion, is not utterly extinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong prescriptive prohibition: invoking the Divine Name in casual anger, mirth, or comedic phrases is profane and an affront to reason and religion. For writers and wits, this is given as a boundary for acceptable humour and rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic technique: juxtapose rural simplicity and town affectation (converted rake sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sober Character of the Husband is dashed with the Man of the Town, and enlivened with those little Cant-phrases which have made my Friend Will Honeycomb often thought very pretty Company... he changed 'Dear Spec.' into 'My Worthy Friend' and subscribed himself 'William Honeycomb'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a satirical device, mix rural virtues (simplicity, health, family responsibility) with residual townly mannerisms and cant to create a comic portrait of conversion or hypocrisy. Small details (forms of address, posture, use of cant) signal character shifts and produce humorous contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical overreaction / fanciful remedies as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: I humbly propose you would invent some Padlock, with full Power under your Hand and Seal, for all modest Persons... to clap upon the Mouths of all such impertinent impudent Fellows: And I wish you would publish a Proclamation, that no modest Person... presume to travel after such a Day without one of them in their Pockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using extravagant, impractical inventions or official-sounding proclamations (padlocks for mouths, seals) to answer social ills is a recognized satirical technique: propose absurd remedies to expose and ridicule improper behaviour. Presented here as humorous moral corrective rather than literal policy.
